title: The Heart of Thankfulness and the Craving Graves
speaker: Elder Jim Blizzard

outline.title: A Thankless Heart Forgets What God Has Given
subpoints: Israel remembered the flavors of Egypt but forgot the slavery and chains.
Discontentment edits the past to make sin look better than God's mercy.
The core issue was craving the gift more than the Giver.

outline.title: Cultivating a Discipline of Noticing Daily Mercies
subpoints: Manna was not flashy but it was faithful and miraculous.
Complaint often stems from blindness to ordinary mercies rather than God's inactivity.
Believers are called to train their hearts to see specific evidences of God's kindness.

outline.title: The Danger of Turning Desire into Demand
subpoints: A desire becomes a demand when one is willing to sin to obtain it.
Entitlement and grumbling expose the idolatry of the heart.
God's 'no' is often a mercy and a protection from spiritual ruin.

outline.title: The Judgment of Kibroth-Hattavah
subpoints: God gave the people what they asked for, resulting in a plague.
Discontentment digs its own grave; indulging in desire without repentance leads to spiritual leanness.
The feast of craving became a funeral, illustrating the cost of pride.

summary:
Elder Jim Blizzard preaches from Numbers 11, focusing on the contrast between a thankful heart and a proud, craving heart. The sermon highlights how the Israelites, despite being redeemed from Egypt and sustained by daily manna, complained and longed for the foods of their former slavery. This discontentment is described as a form of spiritual amnesia, where the people remembered the pleasures of Egypt but forgot the chains and cruelty they endured there. The central theological point is that thankfulness is ruined when the heart craves the gift more than the Giver, leading to a rejection of God's provision and presence.

The message emphasizes the necessity of cultivating a discipline of noticing God's daily mercies. While manna was not luxurious, it was a faithful and miraculous provision that served as a daily sermon on God's care. The sermon argues that complaint often arises not from a lack of provision, but from a blindness to ordinary blessings. Believers are encouraged to actively identify specific instances of God's kindness to train their hearts in contentment and gratitude.

Finally, the sermon addresses the severe consequences of turning desire into demand. When the Israelites demanded meat, God granted their request, but the result was a plague and the naming of the place Kibroth-Hattavah, or 'Graves of Craving.' This serves as a sobering warning that God's 'no' is often a mercy, protecting His people from the spiritual emptiness and judgment that comes from indulging in sinful desires without repentance. The sermon concludes with a call to humble oneself before God, recognizing that true satisfaction is found in the Giver, not just the gifts.
